key_insight: This paper connects cybernetics, interoception, reinforcement learning, and neuroscience to show how autonomous systems can better adapt by tracking their own internal state, not just the external world. The core idea is that embodiment and internal regulation can be treated as part of intelligent decision-making.
problem_solved: Most AI systems optimize actions based mainly on external rewards and observations, but they often lack a mechanism for monitoring internal condition or resource constraints. This work addresses how to build agents that can balance external goals with internal physiological-like signals to stay stable, adaptive, and self-regulating.
method: Builds a framework inspired by living organisms that continuously sense internal state during interaction with the environment.
Combines cybernetic control ideas with reinforcement learning to guide decisions using both external feedback and interoceptive signals.
Uses neuroscience concepts of embodiment to connect perception, internal regulation, and action selection in autonomous agents.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this suggests a path toward more robust agents that can manage energy, stability, safety, and long-horizon adaptation. It is especially relevant for embodied AI, robotics, and autonomous systems operating in changing real-world conditions.
visual_elements: A feedback-loop diagram showing environment, internal state, and action selection
An agent schematic with external sensors and interoceptive sensors
A comparison chart: standard RL vs embodiment-aware RL
Icons representing homeostasis, reward, and adaptation
paper_title: Cybernetics, interoception, and the art of embodiment
